summary:
Orbital Intel is an interactive website that lets anyone explore how nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), a combustion-related air pollutant, changed across 12 major metropolitan regions before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Using monthly Sentinel-5P TROPOMI tropospheric NO₂ column data (2018–2024), users select one or more cities and see a global atmospheric density map with a timeline, longitudinal trend graphs, seasonal cycles, and a statistical summary matrix.

Our analysis compares Jul 2018–Dec 2019 (before), Jan 2020–Dec 2021 (during), and Jan 2022–Dec 2024 (after). London showed the strongest decrease during the pandemic (−22.17%), while Cairo showed the strongest increase (+11.01%). Because seasons, weather, and monsoons strongly shape NO₂, the project keeps seasonal context visible. It also states its limits: satellite columns are not ground-level concentrations, and these patterns do not prove COVID-19 caused the changes.
details:
The project is an interactive data visualization web platform designed to analyze Global Tropospheric NO₂ Dynamics. It tracks nitrogen dioxide atmospheric density across 12 major metropolitan regions (including Cairo, Beijing, London, and New York) from July 2018 through December 2024. It works by fetching and processing raw satellite telemetry, which is then fed into a web-based dashboard. Users can interact with a 3D Earth, use a time slider to view chronological atmospheric density on a 2D map, and compare longitudinal and seasonal NO₂ trends using dynamically generated graphs.

Its benefits:

- Accessibility: It transforms complex, heavy datasets from atmospheric satellites into an intuitive, visually digestible format for researchers and the general public.

- Comparative Analysis: Users can manually select multiple global regions to compare their air quality side-by-side on unified charts.

-cvHistorical Context: By spanning from 2018 to 2024, it provides clear visual evidence of how human behavior—specifically during the COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns and subsequent reopenings—directly impacts tropospheric pollution levels.

The primary impact is to provide a scientifically rigorous yet accessible tool for environmental awareness and policy-making. By cross-referencing satellite observations with World Health Organization (WHO) 2021 Air Quality Guidelines and US EPA health hazard reporting, the project aims to help users, scientists, and policymakers visualize the direct correlation between urban activity and air quality, ultimately supporting data-driven climate and health initiatives.

Programming Languages used:

Python handles the backend logic, data processing, and analysis, while HTML, CSS, and JavaScript power the interactive frontend.

Data Sources & Processing:

The raw atmospheric data is sourced from the Copernicus Sentinel-5P satellite (TROPOMI Level-3 Data) and NASA Earthdata. Google Earth Engine (GEE) is utilized for cloud-based geospatial processing, managed via Python scripts like data_collection.py, data_processing.py, and gee_auth.py.

Frontend Visualization:

The interface uses HTML (index.html) and CSS (design.css) for layout, and JavaScript (design.js) for interactivity. 3D WebGL libraries (like Three.js) are used to render the realistic rotating Earth sphere, while mapping and charting libraries handle the 2D regional maps and dynamic trend graphs.

Statistical Analysis:

Python modules such as statistical_analysis.py and visualizations.py process the raw metrics into usable formats for the frontend tables and charts.

The project merges rigorous scientific data with a highly immersive, cinematic design. Instead of presenting dry, static tables, the dashboard is anchored by a 3D rotating Earth with realistic surface textures, atmospheric lighting, and a dynamic space background featuring stars and depth. It includes an adaptive theme system that maintains this spatial aesthetic in both dark mode and a carefully color-graded, eye-comfortable light mode. Interactive elements like a time slider linked directly to a sequential color scale on the map allow users to physically scrub through time to see pollution move and dissipate.

Our team considered the following while working on the project:

Scientific Integrity: The team prioritized using verified institutional data (Sentinel-5P, WHO, EPA) over simulated metrics.

User Experience (UX): Significant attention was given to visual hierarchy, ensuring background elements like stars do not obscure data or overlap the 3D Earth silhouette. The light mode was specifically engineered with soft neutral backgrounds (#F1F4F7) and muted text to prevent eye strain during extended data analysis.

Modularity: The project structure is heavily compartmentalized. Data ingestion, statistical modeling, configuration, and frontend design are separated into distinct files (e.g., config.py, dashboard.py, design.js) to allow for easy updates and scalable research.
